doc.title: Branford Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: His mother Delores confronts Miss Dewey over low expectations
summary: His mother cursed out his fourth-grade teacher; Branford recalls Dewey's resentment and her son's early death and how his parents taught him to ignore it.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Un-huh. Un-huh. I know your mother’s strong—Delores.
Yeah, she’s combative man, Jesus. Angry black woman there, boy. Yeah, there was always, you know…. There was one time that she went to the school and cursed Miss
Dewey out was because, you know, she didn’t care about none of that other stuff. Like she wasn’t …. We were learning plurals, or something like that, and I said fishes….
This is when you were young.
I was in the fourth grade. Fishes and, you know….

“Do’s” instead of “does.” And I came home and I said, “He do’s that all the time.” And she goes, “No, it’s ’does’ honey.” I said, “No it’s not, it’s ‘do’s.’” So she said, “Who told you that?” I said, “Well Miss Dewey, I said it today and she didn’t correct me.” So my mother went to the school and let her have it. Cause her whole vibe was, well you know, “Well, look at him? You need to lower your expectations.” And my mother went off.
Miss Dewey said this to your mother, “Look at him. You need to lower your….” That’s what the teacher told your mother?

She might not have said, “You need to lower your expectations.” But she said like, “Well, look, you know, c’mon, really? Yeah.” She wasn’t really…she really didn’t…she was one of the people who really resented having to teach black kids. And, you know, she didn’t say too much. She didn’t make my life a living hell, but she didn’t really…. She likes to believe that we were incapable of learning. And then her son was this really talented quarterback who played, Blaise Dewey [?]. He played for LSU and he just developed some weird ass cancer. In the sixties, man, that’s you know, that’s a death sentence. And he died, she was never the same after that. [And] I felt bad for her. I felt bad for her, so it was never one of those things where their behavior caused a tremendous amount of animosity in me.
Mostly I think because my parents were just like, you know…. You don’t let them define you. They do what they do. You just focus on you.
